G2A01.why: By convention, SSB voice above 10 MHz uses upper sideband, so 20 meters (14 MHz) and up use USB.

src.quote: For SSB phone operations below 10 MHz use lower sideband (LSB); above 10 MHz use upper sideband (USB).

G2A02.why: By convention, SSB voice below 10 MHz uses lower sideband, so 160, 75 and 40 meters use LSB.

src.quote: For SSB phone operations below 10 MHz use lower sideband (LSB); above 10 MHz use upper sideband (USB).

G2A03.why: VHF and UHF are far above 10 MHz, and SSB there uses upper sideband by convention.

src.quote: For SSB phone operations below 10 MHz use lower sideband (LSB); above 10 MHz use upper sideband (USB).

G2A04.why: 17 meters (18 MHz) and 12 meters (24 MHz) are above 10 MHz, so voice there uses upper sideband by convention.

src.quote: For SSB phone operations below 10 MHz use lower sideband (LSB); above 10 MHz use upper sideband (USB).

G2A05.why: Single sideband is the standard voice mode on the HF amateur bands, because it packs a lot of power into a narrow slice of spectrum.

src.quote: SSB packs a great deal of power into a small slice of the radio spectrum, allowing many more conversations to occupy the same band

G2A06.why: With the carrier and one sideband removed, SSB uses less bandwidth than AM and puts all its power into the part that carries the voice. It doesn't sound high-fidelity and isn't especially immune to noise.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 17: Radio-Frequency Communications Principles (NAVEDTRA 14189)
src.quote: By eliminating the carrier and one of the sidebands, intelligence is transmitted at a savings in power and frequency bandwidth.

G2A07.why: SSB transmits only one sideband; both the carrier and the other sideband are suppressed. No rule makes SSB the only voice mode on any band.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 17: Radio-Frequency Communications Principles (NAVEDTRA 14189)
src.quote: In a single-sideband transmitter (ssb), only one of the sidebands, the upper or the lower, is transmitted while the remaining sideband and the carrier are suppressed.

G2A08.why: To join a conversation, wait for a pause between transmissions and say your call sign once. Save "break" for emergencies.

src.quote: The best approach is to wait for one station to stop transmitting and then quickly announce your call sign
you should only say “break” when you need to interrupt because of an emergency.

G2A09.why: Using LSB on 160, 75 and 40 meters is simply the accepted convention. Neither sideband is more efficient, the rules allow both, and neither works with an AM detector.

src.quote: For SSB phone operations below 10 MHz use lower sideband (LSB); above 10 MHz use upper sideband (USB).

G2A10.why: VOX (voice-operated switch) puts the transmitter on the air when you start speaking, so you don't have to press a button: hands-free operation. It doesn't change bandwidth, power or audio quality.

src.quote: When the VOX is on, the sound of your voice will automatically switch the transceiver into the transmit mode.

G2A11.why: "CQ DX" asks for long-distance (DX) stations. For a station in the lower 48 states, that means anyone outside the lower 48 states should answer.

G2A12.why: The ALC meter shows how hard you're driving the transmitter. If the reading is too high, turn down the microphone (transmit audio) gain.

src.quote: If the meter indicates that your voice is bouncing it out of the ALC range, you’ll need to find the microphone gain control and turn it down or try speaking a little softer.

G2B01.why: No station has exclusive use of any frequency. Stations must cooperate in choosing channels, and only emergency communications get priority.

src.quote: No frequency will be assigned for the exclusive use of any station.
(c) At all times and on all frequencies, each control operator must give priority to stations providing emergency communications

G2B02.why: Emergency communications get priority, so acknowledge the station in distress and find out what help is needed. Going silent or just turning down your power doesn't help them.

src.quote: (c) At all times and on all frequencies, each control operator must give priority to stations providing emergency communications

G2B03.why: No one owns a frequency, and the rules require stations to cooperate in choosing channels. When propagation brings in another group, work it out with them in a mutually acceptable way.

src.quote: (b) Each station licensee and each control operator must cooperate in selecting transmitting channels and in making the most effective use of the amateur service frequencies.

G2B04.why: A CW signal is only a few hundred hertz wide at most (band plans assume up to 200 Hz), so 150 to 500 Hz of separation keeps you out of a neighbor's receiver passband.

G2B05.why: An SSB voice signal is about 2.7 kHz wide, so stay 2 to 3 kHz away from other stations so your signals don't overlap.

src.quote: Bandwidth: 2700Hz = 2.7 kHz 2K70J3E

G2B06.why: Even if a frequency sounds clear, someone you can't hear may be using it. Ask first: send "QRL?" and your call on CW, or ask "Is the frequency in use?" and your call on phone.

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R M.1172, Miscellaneous abbreviations and signals (Q code)
src.quote: QRL Are you busy? I am busy (or I am busy with … (name and/or call sign)). Please do not interfere.
If the frequency seems clear, ask if the frequency is in use, followed by your call.

G2B07.why: Band plans are voluntary agreements on where each mode and activity goes in a band. Following them is accepted good practice. Listening for two minutes or sending your call three times isn't a standard practice.

src.quote: The IARU Region 2 has established this voluntary band plan to better organize the use of our bands efficiently.

G2B08.why: 50.100–50.125 MHz is the 6-meter DX window. Stations in the 48 contiguous states should use it only for contacts with stations outside the 48 states.

src.quote: 50.10-50.125 DX window
50.100-50.125 2700 CW, SSB DX window.

G2B09.why: Only a person holding an FCC-issued amateur license (and enrolled with a civil defense organization) may be the control operator of a station transmitting in RACES. Government officials without a license may not.

src.quote: No person may be the control operator of an amateur station transmitting in RACES unless that person holds a FCC-issued amateur operator license and is certified by a civil defense organization as enrolled in that organization.

G2B10.why: A net should have a backup frequency so it can move if interference or poor conditions make the main one unusable. Multiple phonetics and reading the whole roster just waste time.

G2B11.why: RACES training drills and tests may not exceed 1 hour per week in total, unless the state's chief emergency planning officer approves longer drills (up to 72 hours, no more than twice a year).

src.quote: Such drills and tests may not exceed a total time of 1 hour per week. With the approval of the chief officer for emergency planning in the applicable State, Commonwealth, District or territory, however, such tests and drills may be conducted for a period not to exceed 72 hours no more than twice in any calendar year.

G2C01.why: With full break-in (QSK), the radio switches to receive between dots, dashes and characters, so you can hear the other station (or interference) while you send.

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R M.1172, Miscellaneous abbreviations and signals (Q code)
src.quote: QSK Can you hear me between your I can hear you between my signals; signals and if so may I break in break in on my transmission. on your transmission?

G2C02.why: QRS means "send more slowly." Formally QRS? is the question "Shall I send more slowly?", but on the air hams commonly use QRS or QRS? to ask the other station to slow down. So the right response is to send slower.

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R M.1172, Miscellaneous abbreviations and signals (Q code)
src.quote: QRS Shall I send more slowly? Send more slowly ( … words per minute).

G2C03.why: KN at the end of a transmission means only the station (or stations) you're in contact with should answer. Others shouldn't break in.

src.quote: KN Used at the end of any transmission when only the specific station contacted is invited to answer.

G2C04.why: QRL means "I am busy." Sent as a question, QRL? asks whether the frequency is in use.

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R M.1172, Miscellaneous abbreviations and signals (Q code)
src.quote: QRL Are you busy? I am busy (or I am busy with … (name and/or call sign)). Please do not interfere.

G2C05.why: Answer at a speed you can copy comfortably, but no faster than the station calling CQ is sending.

src.quote: Don’t send faster than you can receive and don’t respond to a CQ at a speed faster than the other station is sending.

G2C06.why: Zero beating means setting your transmit frequency to match the station you're answering, so you're on the same frequency.

src.quote: When answering a CQer you should zero beat the other ham's frequency. That means setting your transmit frequency as close to theirs as possible.

G2C07.why: In an RST report, a "C" suffix means the signal is chirpy: its frequency shifts slightly as it is keyed. "K" means key clicks and "X" means crystal-steady.

src.quote: If there is a chirp, the letter C may be added to so indicate. Similarly for a click, add K.

G2C08.why: AR marks the end of a message. (SK ends the contact, BK means break, and KN invites only the station you're working.)

src.cite: ARRL, FSD-218 Pocket guide to message handling
src.quote: AR End of message (end of record copy).

G2C09.why: QSL means "I am acknowledging receipt": I received and understood. A QSL card is a written confirmation of a contact, named after this.

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R M.1172, Miscellaneous abbreviations and signals (Q code)
src.quote: QSL Can you acknowledge receipt? I am acknowledging receipt.

G2C10.why: QRN means "I am troubled by static" (natural noise such as lightning crashes). QRM is interference from other stations.

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R M.1172, Miscellaneous abbreviations and signals (Q code)
src.quote: QRN Are you troubled by static? I am troubled by static

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R M.1172, Miscellaneous abbreviations and signals (Q code)
src.quote: QRV Are you ready? I am ready.

G2D01.why: Under an agreement between the FCC and ARRL, trained, vetted volunteers formally monitor the bands and collect evidence of rule violations (and of exemplary operating).

src.quote: The ARRL Volunteer Monitor program is a formal agreement between the FCC and ARRL. Volunteers trained and vetted by ARRL monitor the airwaves and collect evidence that can be used both to correct misconduct or recognize exemplary on-air operation.

G2D02.why: The program's aim is to encourage hams to follow the rules and police themselves. Evidence can be used to correct misconduct, and only flagrant cases are referred to the FCC.

src.quote: collect evidence that can be used both to correct misconduct or recognize exemplary on-air operation. Cases of flagrant violations are referred to the FCC by ARRL for action in accordance with FCC guidelines.

G2D03.why: Monitors at different locations each point a directional antenna at the strongest signal on the repeater input. Where their bearings cross is roughly where the transmitter is (triangulation). The repeater output doesn't help, since it comes from the repeater.

G2D04.why: An azimuthal (equidistant) projection is centered on one location and shows true bearings and distances from that point, so you can read off where to aim a beam. Land shapes far from the center are badly distorted.

G2D05.why: To call any station, repeat "CQ" a few times, say "this is" and your call sign a few times, then pause to listen. Repeat as needed, and keep the call short.

src.quote: To start a contact, call "CQ" or answer someonecalling CQ. A CQ is a general call to get a random contact.
“CQ CQ Calling CQ. This is AD5UAP, Alfa-Delta-Five-Uniform-Alfa-Papa.”

G2D06.why: The long path goes the other way around the Earth along the same great circle, so you point the antenna 180 degrees from the short-path heading.

G2D07.why: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta are the start of the ITU (NATO) phonetic alphabet. The ITU's own list spells the first one "Alfa." Able/Baker and Adam/Boy are older or non-standard lists.

src.quote: A--Alfa B--Bravo C--Charlie D--Delta

G2D08.why: The FCC doesn't require a station log, but a log helps if the FCC (or a neighbor's interference complaint) asks about your station's operation.

src.quote: The Federal Communications Commission does not require hams to keep station logs with records of every contact, but contest sponsors do.
Legally, a log of your transmissions would be invaluable in proving your innocence in an interference complaint.

G2D09.why: Contest rules don't override FCC rules: you must still identify normally (at the end of each contact and at least every 10 minutes). Submitting a log and sending QSLs are optional.

src.quote: (a) Each amateur station, except a space station or telecommand station, must transmit its assigned call sign on its transmitting channel at the end of each communication, and at least every 10 minutes during a communication

G2D10.why: QRP means low-power operation, from the Q signal "decrease transmitter power."

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R M.1172, Miscellaneous abbreviations and signals (Q code)
src.quote: QRP Shall I decrease transmitter power? Decrease transmitter power.
QRP – Q signal referring to low power operations.

G2D11.why: Exchanging signal reports right away tells each station how well it's being heard, so both can adjust: speak or send more slowly, repeat information, or keep the contact short.

G2E02.why: VARA is a high-performance HF data modem (based on OFDM) that Winlink uses to send email over the air.

src.cite: Winlink, Frequently asked questions about Winlink 2000 (2020)

src.cite: WSJT-X User Guide, FT8 tutorial (source mirror on GitHub)
src.quote: TIP: To avoid QRM from competing callers, it is usually best to answer a CQ on a different frequency from that of the CQing station.

G3A01.why: More sunspots go with more solar ultraviolet and X-ray output, which makes the ionosphere denser. A denser ionosphere can refract higher frequencies, so the upper HF bands open more often.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Ionosphere
src.quote: The amount of energy (photon flux) at EUV and x-ray wavelengths varies by nearly a factor of ten over the 11 year solar cycle. The density of the ionosphere changes accordingly.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, F10.7 cm radio emissions
src.quote: The F10.7 correlates well with the sunspot number as well as a number of UltraViolet (UV) and visible solar irradiance records.

G3A02.why: A sudden ionospheric disturbance comes from a solar flare's X-rays, which boost the D region on the daylit side. The D region absorbs lower frequencies more strongly, so those are hit hardest.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Solar flares (radio blackouts)
src.quote: When a strong enough solar flare occurs, ionization is produced in the lower, more dense layers of the ionosphere (the D-layer), and radio waves that interact with electrons in layers lose energy due to the more frequent collisions that occur in the higher density environment of the D-layer.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: As a frequency is lowered, absorption of the radio wave increases. A wave whose frequency is too low is absorbed to such an extent that it is too weak for reception.

G3A03.why: A flare's ultraviolet and X-rays travel at the speed of light, so they arrive when we see the flare: about 8 minutes after leaving the Sun (150 million km ÷ 300,000 km/s ≈ 500 s).

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Solar flares (radio blackouts)
src.quote: The sudden outburst of electromagnetic energy travels at the speed of light, therefore any effect upon the sunlit side of Earth’s exposed outer atmosphere occurs at the same time the event is observed.

G3A04.why: With low solar activity the ionosphere is thin, and the maximum usable frequency often stays below the highest bands. So 15, 12 and 10 meters are the least reliable for long-distance contacts.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Ionosphere
src.quote: The amount of energy (photon flux) at EUV and x-ray wavelengths varies by nearly a factor of ten over the 11 year solar cycle. The density of the ionosphere changes accordingly.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: the higher the frequency of a radio wave, the lower the rate of refraction by an ionized layer.

G3A05.why: The solar flux index (F10.7) measures the Sun's radio emission at a wavelength of 10.7 cm (2800 MHz). It tracks overall solar activity and the sunspot number.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, F10.7 cm radio emissions
src.quote: The solar radio flux at 10.7 cm (2800 MHz) is an excellent indicator of solar activity.

G3A06.why: A geomagnetic storm is a temporary, major disturbance of Earth's magnetic field and magnetosphere, driven by the solar wind.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Geomagnetic storms
src.quote: A geomagnetic storm is a major disturbance of Earth's magnetosphere that occurs when there is a very efficient exchange of energy from the solar wind into the space environment surrounding Earth.

G3A07.why: Even near solar minimum, the daytime maximum usable frequency usually stays above 14 MHz, so 20 meters supports long-distance contacts in daylight at any point in the cycle.

G3A08.why: Geomagnetic storms send charged particles into the polar ionosphere, which absorbs and disrupts HF signals. Paths through high latitudes suffer most.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, HF radio communications
src.quote: During auroral displays, the precipitating electrons can enhance other layers of the ionosphere and have similar disrupting and blocking effects on radio communication.

G3A09.why: Strong geomagnetic activity produces auroras, and the ionized auroral regions can reflect VHF signals, allowing contacts that are otherwise impossible.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Aurora
src.quote: During major geomagnetic storms these ovals expand away from the poles such that aurora can be seen over most of the United States.

src.cite: G. Lange-Hesse, VHF bistatic aurora communications (NASA Technical Reports Server)
src.quote: Radio amateurs discovered during 1939 in the U.S.A. that they were able to communicate abnormally long distances up to about 1000 km on frequencies too high to be propagated by normal modes.

G3A10.why: The Sun rotates about every 27 days as seen from Earth, so active regions and coronal holes face Earth again roughly every 26 to 28 days, and conditions tend to repeat on that cycle.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Coronal holes
src.quote: The more persistent coronal holes can sometimes last through several solar rotations (27-day periods).

G3A11.why: A coronal mass ejection is a cloud of plasma, much slower than light. The fastest reach Earth in about 15 to 18 hours; slower ones take several days.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Coronal mass ejections
src.quote: The fastest Earth-directed CMEs can reach our planet in as little as 15-18 hours. Slower CMEs can take several days to arrive.

G3A12.why: The K-index rates disturbance of Earth's magnetic field over a 3-hour period, on a 0–9 scale. It's a short-term measure of geomagnetic stability.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Station K and A indices
src.quote: The indices have a range from 0 to 9 and are directly related to the maximum amount of fluctuation (relative to a quiet day) in the geomagnetic field over a three-hour interval.

G3A13.why: The A-index averages a day's eight 3-hourly readings into one number, so it describes the longer-term (daily) stability of Earth's magnetic field.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Station K and A indices
src.quote: The value is calculated as the average of eight, three-hourly station ak-indices observed during a UT day, and provides a single, average value to indicate the activity level for that day.

G3A14.why: Coronal holes release high-speed solar wind streams that can cause geomagnetic storms, which disturb HF communication.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Coronal holes
src.quote: Strong CIRs and the faster CH HSS can impact Earth’s magnetosphere enough to cause periods of geomagnetic storming to the G1-G2 (Minor to Moderate) levels

G3B01.why: The long path is much longer than the short path, so the same signal arrives a fraction of a second later by the long path, heard as a slight echo.

G3B02.why: The MUF depends on how dense the ionosphere is along the path, and on the path's length and location. Density changes with time of day, season, solar radiation and disturbances, so all of these affect the MUF.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: It is a very variable layer and its height and density change with time of day, season, and sunspot activity.

G3B03.why: Frequencies just below the MUF are still returned to Earth, and absorption in the lower ionosphere falls as frequency rises. So the highest usable frequency has the least attenuation.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: As a frequency is lowered, absorption of the radio wave increases. A wave whose frequency is too low is absorbed to such an extent that it is too weak for reception.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: This frequency is known as the MAXIMUM USABLE FREQUENCY (muf).

G3B04.why: Automated receiving networks (such as the Reverse Beacon Network or PSK Reporter) report where your signal is being heard right now, so you can see where the band is open from your station.

G3B05.why: Between the LUF and the MUF, the ionosphere refracts signals back to Earth without absorbing too much of them. That's the usable window for that path.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: This frequency is known as the MAXIMUM USABLE FREQUENCY (muf).

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: As a frequency is lowered, absorption of the radio wave increases. A wave whose frequency is too low is absorbed to such an extent that it is too weak for reception.

G3B06.why: Below the LUF, absorption (mostly in the D region) weakens the signal too much to be heard at the destination.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: As a frequency is lowered, absorption of the radio wave increases. A wave whose frequency is too low is absorbed to such an extent that it is too weak for reception.

G3B07.why: LUF is the Lowest Usable Frequency for communication between two specific points.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: there is also a minimum operating frequency. This is known as the LOWEST USABLE FREQUENCY (luf).

G3B08.why: MUF is the Maximum Usable Frequency for communication between two points.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: there is a maximum frequency that can be used for communications between two given locations. This frequency is known as the MAXIMUM USABLE FREQUENCY (muf).

G3B09.why: The F2 region is the highest, about 300 km or more up. A signal leaving at a very low angle can come back down about 4,000 km (roughly 2,500 miles) away in one hop.

G3B10.why: The E region is lower (about 100 km), so one E hop covers less ground: up to about 1,200 miles.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: The E layer refracts hf waves during the day up to 20 megahertz to distances of about 1200 miles.

G3B11.why: If the lowest usable frequency is above the maximum usable frequency, no frequency works: anything low enough to be refracted is absorbed. Ordinary skywave can't cover that path.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: This frequency is known as the MAXIMUM USABLE FREQUENCY (muf).

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: As a frequency is lowered, absorption of the radio wave increases. A wave whose frequency is too low is absorbed to such an extent that it is too weak for reception.

G3B12.why: Thunderstorms are most common in summer, and lightning noise is strongest at lower frequencies, so summer brings heavy static on the lower HF bands.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Likewise, atmospheric noise is greater at lower frequencies; thus, a low-frequency radio wave may have an unacceptable signal-to-noise ratio.

G3C01.why: The D region is the lowest part of the ionosphere, roughly 30 to 55 miles up.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: The D layer ranges from about 30 to 55 miles. Ionization in the D layer is low because it is the lowest region of the ionosphere.

G3C02.why: The critical frequency is the highest frequency a layer will refract back to Earth. It is usually quoted for a wave sent straight up; at more oblique angles (lower elevation, farther from vertical), higher frequencies can return.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: The CRITICAL FREQUENCY is the maximum frequency that a radio wave can be transmitted vertically and still be refracted back to Earth.

G3C03.why: F2 is the highest region, so a wave refracted there comes down farther away than one turned back by the lower E region.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: The F2 layer is the most important layer for long distance hf communications.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: The F layer exists from about 90 to 240 miles.

G3C04.why: Waves sent up too steeply pass through the ionosphere and are lost. The critical angle is the highest takeoff angle that still returns to Earth under the current conditions.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Any wave that leaves the antenna at an angle greater than the critical angle will penetrate the ionospheric layer for that frequency and then be lost in space.

G3C05.why: In daylight the D region forms and absorbs lower HF signals (160, 80, 60 and 40 m) before they reach the higher layers. It disappears at night, so these bands open up for long distances after dark.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: The D layer reflects vlf waves; is important for long range vlf communications; refracts lf and mf waves for short range communications; absorbs hf waves; has little effect on vhf and above; and disappears at night.

G3C06.why: HF scatter signals arrive by many paths at once, each with a different delay, so they sound fluttery or hollow.

G3C07.why: Energy is scattered into the skip zone along several different paths. The copies arrive with different delays and mix together, which distorts the signal.

G3C08.why: Only a small fraction of the signal's energy is scattered back into the skip zone, so scatter signals there are weak.

G3C09.why: The skip zone lies beyond ground-wave range but short of where the skywave first comes down. Normally nothing is heard there, but scattering can put some signal into it.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: The SKIP ZONE is a zone of silence between the point where the ground wave becomes too weak for reception and the point where the sky wave is first returned to Earth.

G3C10.why: NVIS sends MF or HF signals almost straight up. Below the critical frequency they come back down over a wide area around the station, covering short distances (up to a few hundred miles) with no skip zone.

G3C11.why: The D region is the most absorbent of lower HF signals (below about 10 MHz) in daytime.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: The D layer reflects vlf waves; is important for long range vlf communications; refracts lf and mf waves for short range communications; absorbs hf waves; has little effect on vhf and above; and disappears at night.

On 10 meters, repeaters are allowed only above 29.5 MHz.

G1B.intro: Antenna structures, beacons, permitted one-way transmissions and retransmissions, and the catch-all of good engineering and good amateur practice.

facts.text: Antenna structures over 200 feet, or near a public-use airport, need FAA notification and FCC registration.
PRB-1: state and local rules must reasonably accommodate amateur radio and be the minimum practicable regulation.
Beacons are for observing propagation and reception.
Beacon power is limited to 100 W.
A beacon may use only one channel per band from one location.
On HF, beacons may run under automatic control only on 28.20–28.30 MHz.
Any station may occasionally retransmit US government weather and propagation forecasts.
Abbreviations and Q signals are fine; codes meant to obscure meaning are not.
Anything not covered by the rules must follow good engineering and good amateur practice.

facts.text: The general limit is 1500 W PEP output.
30 meters (10.10–10.15 MHz) is limited to 200 W PEP.
Power is measured as PEP: the average power during one RF cycle at the peak of the modulation.
On 60 m, emissions must be no wider than 2.8 kHz.
60 m power is limited in ERP relative to a dipole, so keep antenna gain records if you use something else.
Data techniques may be used if their technical characteristics are publicly documented.

G1D.intro: Volunteer Examiners and exam credit, operating on a new CSCE, and remote operation across borders.

facts.text: Exams are given by at least three VEs, accredited by a VEC.
VEs must be at least 18.
VEs must never have had a license revoked or suspended. There's no citizenship requirement.
General VEs may give Technician exams only.
A CSCE gives element credit for 365 days.
With a CSCE you may use the new privileges right away, until the application is processed or 365 days pass.
Until the upgrade appears, a new General identifies with "/AG" when using General privileges.
A former General (past the grace period) gets Element 3 credit but must pass Element 2 again.
A US station's control operator needs a US license (or FCC reciprocal authorization), wherever they control it from.

G1E.intro: Third-party traffic, repeaters, ITU regions, spread spectrum, and automatically controlled digital stations.

facts.text: A third party whose amateur license was revoked (and not reinstated) can't take part.
International messages are limited to amateur radio topics and remarks of a personal character.
North and South America are ITU Region 2.
Spread spectrum is limited to 10 W PEP.
Spread spectrum must not cause harmful interference to other emissions, and must accept interference from them.
Automatically controlled digital stations may talk to each other on 6 m and up, and in small HF segments.
Elsewhere, they may only answer a station under local or remote control.
Avoid the NCDXF/IARU beacon frequencies (14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930, 28.200 MHz).

G2A.intro: Phone operating on HF. Single sideband is the main voice mode: lower sideband below 10 MHz and upper sideband above, by convention rather than rule. Also covered: joining a conversation, VOX, ALC and answering DX calls.

facts.text: SSB sends only one sideband; the carrier and the other sideband are suppressed.
Dropping the carrier and one sideband saves both power and bandwidth compared with AM.
Convention: LSB below 10 MHz (160, 75, 40 m), USB above (20 m and up, VHF/UHF). 60 m is the exception and uses USB.
To join a conversation, say your call sign once between transmissions. "Break" is for emergencies.
VOX switches to transmit when you speak, for hands-free operation.
If the ALC reading is too high, turn down the microphone gain.

G2B.intro: Sharing the bands: nobody owns a frequency, emergencies come first, how far apart to stay from other signals, voluntary band plans, nets and RACES.

facts.text: No frequency is assigned for any station's exclusive use; stations must cooperate.
Emergency communications always get priority.
An SSB voice signal is about 2.7 kHz wide, so stay 2–3 kHz from other SSB stations.
CW signals are much narrower (band plans allow 200 Hz), so 150–500 Hz of separation is enough.
Before calling CQ, ask whether the frequency is in use ("QRL?" on CW).
Band plans are voluntary, but following them is good amateur practice.
50.100–50.125 MHz is the 6-meter DX window, for contacts with stations outside the 48 contiguous states.
A RACES control operator must hold an FCC amateur license and be enrolled with a civil defense organization.
RACES drills and tests are limited to 1 hour per week.

G2C.intro: CW operating: full break-in, Q signals and prosigns, matching speed and frequency, and RST reports. A Q signal followed by a question mark asks the question; without it, it gives the answer.

facts.text: QSK (full break-in): you hear the other station between your own dots and dashes.
QRS: send more slowly.
QRL: I am busy. QRL? asks if the frequency is in use.
QSL: I acknowledge receipt.
QRN: I am troubled by static.
QRV: I am ready.
KN: only the station you're working should answer.
AR: end of message.
RST suffixes: C for chirp, K for key clicks, X for crystal-steady.
Zero beat the station you answer, and don't send faster than it does.

G2D.intro: The Volunteer Monitor program, aiming a beam, calling CQ, phonetics, logs, contests and QRP. An azimuthal (equidistant) map centered on your station shows true bearings and distances to anywhere, so you can read off where to point. The long path goes the other way around the Earth, 180° from the short-path heading.

facts.text: Volunteer Monitors are trained volunteers, under an FCC–ARRL agreement, who monitor the bands and collect evidence of rule violations.
The ITU phonetic alphabet starts Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta.
The FCC doesn't require a log, but contest sponsors do.
Contest or not, identify at the end of each contact and every 10 minutes.
QRP means low-power operation.

G2E.intro: Digital modes on HF: RTTY, FT8 and other WSJT-X modes, Winlink with PACTOR and VARA, and AREDN mesh networks.

facts.text: Amateur RTTY: 170 Hz shift, sent on lower sideband by convention.
FT8 and other WSJT-X modes are sent on upper sideband.
FT8 uses 15-second transmit/receive periods, so your clock must be within about 1 second of UTC.
The 20-meter FT8 dial frequency is 14.074 MHz.
Answer an FT8 CQ in the opposite (odd or even) time slot.
Call on a clear frequency rather than right on top of the CQing station.
A Winlink RMS is a gateway between radio users and internet email.
VARA is a high-performance HF modem used with Winlink.
AREDN builds high-speed data networks for emergencies and events.

G3A.intro: The Sun drives HF propagation. Its ultraviolet and X-rays ionize the upper atmosphere, and that output rises and falls over the roughly 11-year sunspot cycle. Flares, coronal mass ejections and coronal holes can disrupt conditions, and the K and A indices rate how disturbed Earth's magnetic field is.

facts.text: Sunspot numbers and the Sun's ultraviolet output rise and fall together; both track the F10.7 index.
Solar EUV and X-ray output varies about tenfold over the 11-year cycle, and the ionosphere's density follows it. A denser ionosphere supports higher usable frequencies.
The solar flux index is the Sun's radio output at 10.7 cm (2800 MHz).
A flare's X-rays arrive at the speed of light (about 8 minutes) and boost D-region absorption on the daylit side: a sudden ionospheric disturbance.
Coronal mass ejections take 15 hours to several days to arrive.
Coronal holes send high-speed solar wind that can trigger geomagnetic storms, and can recur with the Sun's 27-day rotation.
Auroras can reflect VHF signals far beyond normal range.
Geomagnetic storms disrupt HF, especially at high latitudes.
K-index: geomagnetic disturbance over 3 hours, 0 to 9.
A-index: the day's average, a longer-term measure.

G3B.intro: For any path at any moment there is a window of usable frequencies. Above the maximum usable frequency (MUF), signals pass through the ionosphere. Below the lowest usable frequency (LUF), they are absorbed. The best signals are just below the MUF. One hop off the E region covers up to about 1,200 miles; off the higher F2 region, about 2,500 miles.

facts.text: MUF: the maximum usable frequency between two points. Higher frequencies are refracted less.
LUF: below it, absorption makes the signal too weak to receive.
The F2 layer, and so the MUF, varies with time of day, season and solar activity.
One E-region hop reaches about 1,200 miles.
Atmospheric noise is worse at lower frequencies, which is why summer static is heavy on the low bands.

G3C.intro: The ionosphere's regions, from lowest to highest, are D, E, F1 and F2. The D region absorbs; the F2 region carries the longest skip. Also covered: critical frequency and angle, the skip zone and scatter, and NVIS.

facts.text: The D region is the lowest region of the ionosphere.
In daytime the D region absorbs HF (worst on the lower bands). It disappears at night.
F2 is the main layer for long-distance HF.
The F layer is the highest (about 90 to 240 miles up), so it gives the longest hops.
Critical frequency: the highest frequency a layer returns to Earth (for a wave sent straight up).
Critical angle: waves leaving at steeper angles go through the layer and are lost.
Skip zone: the silent gap between ground-wave range and the first skywave landing. Weak, fluttery scatter signals can sometimes be heard there.
